## Developing Robust Clinical Text Deep Learning Models - A "Painless" Approach

Yutong WUa,1, James A HUGHESb,c, Anna-Lisa LYRSTEDTc, Sarah HAZELWOODd, Nathan J BROWNc,e, Lee JONESf, Clint DOUGLASb,g, Rajeev JARUGULAd, Kevin CHUc,e and Anthony NGUYENa a The Australian e-Health Research Centre, CSIRO, Brisbane, Australia b School of Nursing, Centre for Healthcare Transformation, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Australia c Emergency and Trauma Centre, Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, Brisbane, Australia d Emergency Department, The Prince Charles Hospital, Brisbane, Australia e Faculty of Medicine, University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia f School of Public Health and Social Work, Queensland University of Technology, Brisbane, Australia g Metro North Health, Brisbane, Australia

Abstract. The success of deep learning in natural language processing relies on ample labelled training data. However, models in the health domain often face data inadequacy due to the high cost and difficulty of acquiring training data. Developing such models thus requires robustness and performance on new data. A generalised incremental multiphase framework is proposed for developing robust and performant clinical text deep learning classifiers. It incorporates incremental multiphases for training data size assessments, cross-validation setup to avoid test data bias, and robustness testing through inter/intra-model significance analysis. The framework's effectiveness and generalisation were confirmed by the task of identifying patients presenting in ‘pain’ to the emergency department.

Keywords. Pain, deep learning, emergency department, language model, triage nurse assessment, text classification

## 1. Introduction

Deep learning models are gaining traction in improving natural language processing (NLP) for medical and clinical free text [1]. While larger training datasets are thought to enhance model performance [2], their use is often impractical in healthcare. Acquiring labelled clinical data is expensive and labour-intensive, particularly when medical expertise is needed for annotation. These obstacles, stemming from data scarcity, hinder the progress of deep learning applications in the health domain [3]. Active and weakly supervised learning are cost-effective techniques for reducing annotation expenses [2]. probability of being correct. However, these methods do not determine optimal model and dataset sizes for robust and high-performance classifiers. Comparing deep learning models for text-based disease classification via learning curve analysis demonstrated effective fine-tuning of pre-trained models on small datasets, yielding high performance [4]. However, the robustness and performance of these transformer models on new data remain uncertain. This study used a generalised incremental multiphase methodological framework to develop and robustly assess clinical text classifiers. The framework incorporates incremental multiphases for training data size assessment, cross-validation for unbiased testing and inter/intra-model significance testing for robustness. It was applied to identify patients in pain at an emergency department (ED), enabling models for population-level evaluations and real-time patient care interventions. Learning curve analysis evaluated diverse deep learning models, revealing performance-resource tradeoffs considering parameter sets, computational costs, and domain specificity.

## 2. Methods

2.1. Data Description and Problem Formulation

The study utilised the Pain dataset, comprising 10,000 randomly chosen records of clinical data collected from adult patients at an Australian hospital ED between March 2018 and February 20212. Each record includes two free-text data fields: "presenting problem" and "nurse assessment," completed upon patient arrival. Two experienced ED nurses independently labeled each record as "Pain" (if pain symptoms were evident) or "No Pain." Discrepancies were resolved by a third nurse for 957 cases. The dataset contains 5,520 "Pain" and 4,480 "No-Pain" records. The task was formulated as a binary text classification problem, predicting the pain outcome ("Pain" or "No-Pain") based on concatenated triage nurse assessments (two free-text data fields).

2.2. Deep Learning Models

Popular deep learning text classification models ranging from simpler deep learning architectures to more complex transformer-based architectures were evaluated.  Fine-tuned BERT and distilled BERT models: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) are cutting-edge transformer models excelling in diverse NLP tasks [4]. Fine-tuning BERT models allow large pretrained models to be trained on a task-specific dataset. A distillation strategy XtremeDistill [5] was also applied to compress the huge parameter space in BERT models into smaller ones.  Fine-tuned domain specific BlueBERT and distilled BlueBERT models: BlueBERT [6], pre-trained on PubMed abstracts and clinical notes to outperform the original BERT on health domain NLP tasks, was selected to be fine-tuned on the Pain data. XtremedDistill was also applied to build a compressed version of the BlueBERT model.

 Attention-based RNN models (AttRNN): Building upon prior work that introduced a pain classification RNN with pre-trained word and character embeddings [7], Hughes et al. [8] improved performance and interpretability by integrating BERT or BlueBERT embeddings and an attention layer. Given the promising outcomes of AttRNN, we retrained the model on the current Pain dataset to assess its performance with expanded training datasets.

2.3. Proposed Framework

The generalised incremental multiphase framework architecture based on cross validation and significance testing is shown in Figure 1.

*Figure 1. Generalised incremental multiphase framework.*

2.3.1. Incremental Multiphases

The framework comprises incremental model training phases followed by a final evaluation phase. Training phases assess classifier generalisation with increasing dataset sizes, while the evaluation phase validates all generated models. Pain data was split into ten equisized subsets; eight used for the incremental model training phases and 2,000 for final evaluation. Initial phase began with two subsets (2,000 records) for training. Subsequent phases added 1,000 records per phase. The final evaluation validated all models across phases on the reserved 2,000 encounters.

2.3.2. Cross-Validation based Generalisation

At each incremental training phase, k-fold cross validation (CV) assessed model generalisation. Deep learning often faces challenges of performance drop on unseen data, even from the same distribution as training data. While CV can be expensive due to training multiple models, our framework integrates k-fold CV into each training phase to ensure generalisation. In this study, 5-fold CV was utilised. The initial phase trained each model candidate independently with 5 train-validation-test (60:20:20) splits. Subsequent phases repeated 5-fold CV with increasing training data size using trainvalidation splits (80:20), while preserving the initial test split (400 test cases) for consistent cross-phase comparisons.

2.3.3. Inter-model and Intra-model Significance Testing

Statistical significance testing, specifically Approximate Randomisation test [9] with N = 1,000, across all model performances, including intra-model (same model type) and inter-model (across model types) comparisons, was performed to provide evidence for determining if the performance of two model instances were significantly different.

2.4. Evaluation Methodology

The evaluation metric employed was accuracy. In balanced datasets like the Pain dataset, where positive and negative labels are evenly distributed, accuracy sufficed for model assessment. Generalisation was reported as average performance across 5-fold CV (across all 400 test cases in 5 folds) and final evaluation data (2,000 test cases). Learning curves analysed model performances relative to training data size, while box plots depicted result distribution.

## 3. Results

Model performances and learning curves in Table 1 and Figure 2 show all deep learning models achieving accuracies over 88%, with peak performance at 93%. BlueBERT excelled with larger training datasets, while AttRNN-BlueBERT outperformed in limited datasets, validating AttRNN's proficiency on small datasets [8].

## 4. Discussion

Learning curves showcased performance gains with growing training dataset size, albeit with diminishing returns. BlueBERT's 6,000 training examples matched the performance

of the best model trained with 7,000 examples (p-value > 0.05). Health domain-specific models surpassed general language models in performances based on their respective corpora domains (p-value < 0.05). Distilled models, though slightly less competitive than uncompressed versions (p-value < 0.05), remain valuable in low-resource settings, delivering strong performance with significantly fewer parameters.

## 5. Conclusions

The incremental multiphase framework was effective in generating learning curves to show trends and variability in performances from different models and dataset sizes. Significance testing provided quantitative evidence for robustness assessments and enabled the identification of dataset sizes that produce robust and performant results. Results also confirm the need for domain-specific pre-training and the use of distilled models in low-resourced settings. Proof-of-principle was demonstrated on a clinical classification task and dataset, selected models, and evaluation metrics, but the framework is flexible and adaptable. Active and weakly supervised learning setups can be incorporated, along with online learning strategies for model recalibration whereby new labelled data can be continuously used to monitor and update models accordingly.
